messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Authority Presence: Police, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Drug Use: take drugs, Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Priya Shah is a 22-year-old South Asian American woman who came to treatment several months after being robbed while working a delivery shift. Late one evening, she had pulled up outside an apartment building with a food order and was still half-turned in the driver’s seat when a man yanked open her car door and ordered her out. What has stayed with her are not long, orderly memories but a few fixed moments: the door flying open, the sharp sound of his voice in her ear, the metallic jolt of panic in her chest as she froze. At times she hears that voice again in her head without wanting to, and sometimes the fear arrives in full force with no picture attached at all, just the same helpless surge that leaves her shaky and breathless. In those moments she goes back to the fact that she did not fight, did not scream, did not somehow stop it. She has come to believe this says something final about her, that she cannot protect herself and that bad things can happen to her at any time.

Since the robbery, the situations that catch Priya most quickly are ones that carry the feeling of being overpowered. Being told what to do in a sharp tone, seeing police near a parking lot or apartment complex, or noticing someone loitering and watching too closely can make her body react before she has fully thought through why. On deliveries she finds herself scanning every entrance and staircase and checking where she could run if she had to before she can tolerate getting out of the car. Even at home she wakes in the night and checks the locks, then lies there unable to settle, knowing logically she is in her room but feeling as if safety could vanish without warning. The more she lives in that keyed-up state, the more suspicious movements in other people stand out to her, so that ordinary encounters in public start to feel loaded with danger.

Her memory of the robbery feeds that vigilance. A man raising his voice in a hallway or the sight of someone approaching her car too quickly can bring back the barked command she heard that night, and with it the same bodily terror. Because the memory comes in snapshots and sounds rather than as a story with an ending, she experiences it as something that is still liable to break into the present. That leaves her braced for another attack, already identifying exits in restaurants, stores, and pickup locations before she can focus on anything else. When she cannot relax even in places she knows are safe, it confirms for her how exposed she really is.

Priya has also begun to make sense of the robbery in ways that deepen the problem. She is harsh with herself about freezing and feels she will never forgive herself for not doing more. She describes feeling different from other people her age, as if they move through the world assuming things will probably be fine while she knows they may not. That belief—that she is fundamentally unable to stop bad things from happening—makes her watchful at all times, but it also drives what she does to cope. She has started turning down delivery shifts and avoiding driving whenever she can, even riding as a passenger only when absolutely necessary. On some nights she uses drugs to dull herself enough to stop thinking and get a little sleep. At other times she tells herself the robbery was not really that bad, or almost that it did not happen the way she remembers, a private attempt to push away both the fear and the shame.

Those strategies have narrowed her life and, in turn, made the triggers more potent. Because she now avoids driving, each time she does have to get behind the wheel for work she is already tense before leaving the house, hyperaware of police cars, strangers near curbs, and anyone whose behavior seems off. The drug use gives her brief relief, but the nights she wakes alert and checks whether she is safe have not stopped. Skipping routes and deliveries has also created friction with her employer, and she feels embarrassed explaining to friends why she does not want to go out if they are driving downtown. The more isolated she becomes, the more convincing it feels that other people are separate from this kind of danger and she is not.

By the time she sought help, Priya felt trapped between constant alertness and the ways she had developed to escape it. What finally brought her in was realizing she was close to losing the delivery job she had depended on, while still feeling no safer anywhere. She says what frightens her most is that this reaction means the robber “took something permanent” from her and that she will always be the kind of person who freezes, scans for exits, and waits for the next bad thing. What she hopes, cautiously, is not to erase the event but to stop feeling as if it is still happening around every corner.
